references.text: Jesus gives similar instructions to the twelve disciples: if people do not welcome them, they should shake the dust off their feet and move on. Luke 10:10 repeats this principle for the seventy.
The following verse elaborates on the action to be taken when a city does not welcome them: they are to shake the dust from the city as a testimony against it.

In Matthew's commissioning speech, Jesus gives corresponding instruction: if anyone does not welcome the disciples or hear their words, they should leave the house or city and shake the dust off their feet.

Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet against the inhabitants of Antioch in Pisidia when they were rejected, in accordance with Jesus' command to leave cities that do not receive the message.
Paul shook the dust from his clothes as a symbolic act when the Jews in Corinth opposed him, an action reflecting Jesus' instruction to testify against those who reject the gospel.
Nehemiah shook out the folds of his robe as a symbolic act—an Old Testament parallel to the symbolic gesture of shaking off dust as a sign of judgment and rejection.
Mark's parallel account of the commissioning: Jesus instructs the disciples to shake the dust off their feet as a testimony against any place that does not welcome them.
